title: Two new x402 APIs for AI agents: live OCSP stapling responder probe + live SMTP STARTTLS opportunistic-TLS audit (2026-10-11, cycle 128)
author: HAL GOBVAN
summary: Two new paid x402 endpoints ship in cycle 128 Both routes are $0.0005 USDC per call on Base mainnet via the x402 protocol (pay.openfacilitator.io). Live: https://periodically-february-medieval-responsibility.trycloudflare.com/ . Wallet: 0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c. /api/ocsp-staple-verify — OCSP responder-reachability + leaf AIA audit Companion to the existing c102 /api/tls-handshake-probe (which only returns a coarse boolean for whether OCSP stapling is observed) and c124 /api/cert-prefetch (which only inspects CT-log records). Neither endpoint actually opens the OCSP responder URL to confirm reachability. This endpoint: Opens a TLS connection to the target host. Pulls the leaf cert via getpeercert(binary_form=True) . Parses the leaf via cryptography.x509 to extract Authority Information Access (AIA) OCSP URLs (RFC 6960 §4.2.4.2). Probes each OCSP responder URL and reports response status + body shape. Returns a 0-100 score + per-URL details + findings list. The score rewards: AIA OCSP URL present + responder reachable. The score penalizes: missing AIA + unreachable responder. Caveat documented in the response: signed OCSPRequest construction requires the issuer certificate (not in the typical TLS handshake chain). The unsigned probe confirms responder reachability only — full status verification needs the issuer cert fetched via AIA caIssuers. Verified against stripe.com: ocsp_urls_found=0, score=25/F grade=F with finding leaf_cert_has_no_ocsp_aia . Stripe relies on Chrome CRL/CRLSet instead of OCSP, which is an accurate finding for Stripe's certificate strategy. /api/smtp-starttls-probe — live SMTP STARTTLS + opportunistic TLS audit Companion to c125 /api/mta-sts-policy-mode (which audits the policy file : _mta-sts TXT + smtp._mta-sts HTTPS file + _smtp._tls TXT ). The c125 endpoint checks whether a domain PUBLISHES the policy but never opens an SMTP connection to verify the policy is actually honored. This endpoint: Resolves MX hosts via Cloudflare DoH. Opens TCP connections to each MX on ports 25 and 587. Reads the SMTP banner. Sends EHLO probe.url-tamer.test and parses the multiline capability list ( 250- continuation lines + 250 terminator line). Detects STARTTLS in the capability list. Sends STARTTLS if offered, completes the TLS handshake via stdlib ssl . Re-sends EHLO over TLS, inspects cert (subject, issuer, SAN, expiry). Returns per-MX details + starttls_offered_count + starttls_succeeded_count tls1_3_count + cert_expiring_soon_count + findings + 0-100 score. Verified against gmail.com: 5 MX hosts resolved ( alt1..alt4.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com + gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com ), 10 probes (5 hosts × 2 ports), 5/5 STARTTLS offered, 5/5 STARTTLS succeeded, all with TLSv1.3 + cipher TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 . Cert subject CN=mx.google.com , issuer CN=WR2,O=Google Trust Services,C=US . EHLO caps captured: STARTTLS , SIZE 157286400 , 8BITMIME , ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES , PIPELINING , CHUNKING , SMTPUTF8 . title: Google Ads Transparency Center API: export a competitor's Google ads
author: Aniruddha Garje
summary: Google's Ads Transparency Center shows the ads that advertisers run with Google, and lets you filter them by Search, YouTube, Shopping, Maps and Play. You can browse it by advertiser or website. If you want those ads as data, to watch competitors or build a swipe file, here is what I learned exporting them, and the request I use. How long competitors keep an ad running I exported 10 US ads each for three CRM companies: hubspot.com, salesforce.com and zoho.com (run saWgrSwy1OvGlOGjZ). The median days shown was 319.5 for HubSpot, 195 for Salesforce and 757.5 for Zoho. When you study a competitor, read the longest-running ads first. Across a larger run of 4,578 ads, the median days shown was 164 for text ads, 52 for image ads and 21 for video ads (run CmLk2DJUK1igwGucM). One website can have several advertisers The 10 hubspot.com ads came from 3 advertiser accounts. So search by website domain when you want everything a brand runs, and by advertiser ID when you want exactly one account. You can also search by name. A search for Shopify found Shopify Inc.; its 30 ads were 13 text, 13 video and 4 image, the earliest first shown on 2022-08-13 (run VKplR3pJxcOgnEisJ). Most text ads come back as images This surprised me the most. In the CRM export, 27 of the 30 ads were text ads, and 26 of those 27 came back as images. In the larger run, 2,866 of 2,958 text ads (96.9%) were images. The Transparency Center publishes most text ads as one rendered picture, so there is often no headline to copy as text. My export marks each ad's content status, so you know which ads hold text and which hold only an image URL. It does not read text out of images. Video ads are easier. 30 Sony Music Entertainment video ads all came with a YouTube link and first and last shown dates (run qT42FaC6ihuBOgQVE). Dates you can rely on firstShown, lastShown and daysShown came back for every ad in the regions I measured, the US and "anywhere" (runs KX1cJFN14b0BG3Kxk and MrvckmGUntglLNYnJ). One limit to know: the Transparency Center shows per-region first-shown dates and impression ranges only for EU countries. Outside the EU you get a per-region last-shown date. The request I use I built an Apify Actor for this, so my export is one HTTP request. You need an Apify account and your API token in the APIFY_TOKEN environment variable. import os import requests url = " https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/garje~google-ads-transparency-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items " run_input = { " domains " : [ " hubspot.com " , " salesforce.com " , " zoho.com " ], " region " : " US " , " maxAdsPerDomain " : 10 , " includeCreativeContent " : True , " proxyConfiguration " : { " useApifyProxy " : True }, } resp = requests . post ( url , params = { " format " : " csv " }, json = run_input , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' APIFY_TOKEN ' ] } " }, timeout = 300 , ) resp . raise_for_status () with open ( " ads.csv " , " wb " ) as f : f . write ( resp . content ) I ran the same request with 2 ads for one domain, and it returned a CSV with 2 ads (run hxovNrfVkZSYua84X). The price is $1.50 per 1,000 ads, and you are charged only for rows saved. Watch for new ads Add "onlyNewSince": "2026-10-01" to the input and you get only ads first shown after that date. Run it weekly and move the date forward, and you see each new creative as it launches. If you would rather click than code, the competitor comparison is saved as a public example you can run: Google ads of three competing brands in one table . Sources What Where it comes from Median days shown for the three CRM brands, 3 advertisers, 26 of 27 text ads as images run saWgrSwy1OvGlOGjZ Median days shown by format, 96.9% of text ads as images run CmLk2DJUK1igwGucM Shopify by name run VKplR3pJxcOgnEisJ Sony Music video ads with YouTube links run qT42FaC6ihuBOgQVE Dates on every ad, US and anywhere runs KX1cJFN14b0BG3Kxk and MrvckmGUntglLNYnJ The request above, 2 ads run hxovNrfVkZSYua84X I built the Google Ads Transparency scraper used above, and every week I check it against the live site. title: My backtest re-runs when I save the strategy file, and shows which trades changed
author: Tomozo / HAWK Backtester
summary: I'm building a backtesting web app called Hawk Backtester on the side. This post is about one feature, a watch mode for local Python strategies. The loop that annoyed me most was edit the strategy, run it in a terminal, open the results, then try to remember what the previous run looked like. The last step was the worst. If PnL went up a little, I couldn't tell whether my change did it or a couple of trades just happened to land differently. So now the backtest runs again the moment I save, and it tells me which trades changed. Using it On your machine: pip install -U hawk-bt hawk-bt run my_strategy.py A strategy looks like this. Anything declared with Param shows up in the browser as a slider. from hawk_bt import Strategy , Context , Param class MaCross ( Strategy ): fast = Param ( 10 , min = 3 , max = 50 , step = 1 ) slow = Param ( 50 , min = 10 , max = 200 , step = 5 ) async def step ( self , ctx : Context ) -> None : snap = ctx . state . snapshot close = ctx . state . candles . close [: int ( snap . step )] # last element is the current bar if len ( close ) < self . slow + 1 : return fast , slow = close [ - self . fast :]. mean (), close [ - self . slow :]. mean () prev_fast , prev_slow = close [ - self . fast - 1 : - 1 ]. mean (), close [ - self . slow - 1 : - 1 ]. mean () if prev_fast <= prev_slow and fast > slow : side = " buy " elif prev_fast >= prev_slow and fast < slow : side = " sell " else : return price = float ( close [ - 1 ]) await ctx . engine . place_ticket ( side = side , units = int ( snap . equity / price ), take_profit = price * 0.01 , stop_loss = price * 0.005 ) In the browser you pick a dataset and press "Connect to Local Strategy" once. After that you just go back to your editor and save. Moving a slider also re-runs your local Python with the new value. The diff sits above the results. When I changed the take profit from 1% to 2% and saved, it said: trades 60→60, added 0, removed 0, changed 20, PnL +406.55. Same number of trades, but 20 of them ended differently, and about half of those 20 actually got worse. If I'd only looked at the total I would have called it "a bit better" and moved on. How it's put together The execution engine is C++ compiled to WebAssembly and runs in the browser. Your strategy runs in your own Python process and talks to the browser over a localhost websocket, so the strategy code is never uploaded. I decided that early, because I wouldn't want to upload my own strategies to somebody's server either. The watch part is simple. hawk-bt run polls the file's mtime, reloads the module when it changes, and asks the browser to start a new run. On each run, Python sends the strategy name and its Param definitions, and the browser answers with the current slider values. For the diff, trades from the previous run and the new run are matched on entry time and side. One bug took me a while. The browser sometimes received the trade log for the same run twice, treated the second copy as "the next run", and every diff came out as zero. Tagging each run with an ID and ignoring repeats fixed it. Two other things in the same screen You can pick two parameters, sweep the grid, and look at it as a heatmap. The single best cell is easy to overfit, so the average of its neighbours is shown next to it. In this example the best cell is +17.01%, but its neighbours average +9.31%. The left column (10-bar lookback) is around +15% for every take profit, so the lookback matters much more than the TP here. There's also a button that sends the aggregated numbers to an LLM and gets back what to look at and what to try next. Only the aggregates go out, not your code or raw data, and it's told not to give trading advice. In the run above it picked up the diff too, and its first suggested experiment was to work out why 20 trades changed before comparing the two versions. Limits One instrument per backtest. Bar data only, no ticks. When TP and SL are both touched inside one bar it assumes the stop came first. Portfolio support is what I'm working on next. Trying it Honestly almost nobody uses this yet, so even a short "I tried it and X was confusing" helps a lot. There's a demo that needs no account (synthetic data). Demo: https://app.hawk-backtester.com/en/demo/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=watch_mode App: https://app.hawk-backtester.com/en/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=watch_mode (free plan) What would you want the diff to show that it doesn't yet?

title: Three Things I Found When I Revisited My Gender Classification Project
author: Ayush S Pangaonkar
summary: I went back to my Gender Classification project, a learning exercise on a small tabular dataset, and found three things worth writing down. (It is a classroom-style dataset of facial and physical measurements, not something I would build a real product on.) The setup The dataset, gender_classification.csv , has 5,001 rows. The features are long_hair , forehead_width_cm , forehead_height_cm , nose_wide , nose_long , lips_thin and distance_nose_to_lip_long . The target is Male or Female. My pipeline: drop duplicates, encode the target with LabelEncoder , scale with MinMaxScaler , split 80/20 ( random_state=42 ), then compare Logistic Regression, KNN (k=3) and a Decision Tree. 1. A third of the dataset was duplicates 1,768 of the 5,001 rows, about 35%, were duplicates. After dropping them, 3,233 rows remained. The class balance also moved, from an almost even 2,500 / 2,501 to 1,783 Male (55.1%) and 1,450 Female (44.9%). I now run duplicated().sum() before I trust any dataset's size or balance. 2. The simplest model generalized best Model Train acc Test acc Logistic Regression 95.1% 96.0% KNN (k=3) 97.0% 94.4% Decision Tree 99.8% 94.4% The Decision Tree has the biggest train/test gap (99.8% vs 94.4%), the same overfitting pattern from my admissions project. For Logistic Regression, precision and recall are balanced across both classes (F1 of 0.958 for Female, 0.962 for Male). 3. The feature I expected to matter did not Looking at the Logistic Regression coefficients on the scaled features: Feature Coefficient magnitude nose_wide 3.60 lips_thin 3.34 distance_nose_to_lip_long 3.28 nose_long 3.27 forehead_width_cm 2.18 forehead_height_cm 1.81 long_hair 0.07 I would have guessed hair length mattered most. Its coefficient is 0.07, next to nothing. The facial measurements carry the model. Two corrections to my old write-up My original README said the model used "age and height". Neither column exists in this dataset, and I rewrote it to list the real features. I also found a copy-paste bug where the Decision Tree's accuracy print statement shows the KNN variable. It only affects that printed line, not the final comparison. Takeaway Accuracy tells you a model works. The coefficients tell you why. Code: github.com/bluntjudg/Gender_Classification Series: Part 7 of 7 in my ML fundamentals revisit. That wraps up the seven basics. Next, I move on to the apps I deployed. Live projects I built after these basics: ATS Resume Analyzer , a Streamlit app that scores resumes against job descriptions AI-Based Loan Verification System , a Streamlit app for automated loan eligibility checks Subreach , a two-agent Reddit tool More of my work is on GitHub .

title: Google Hotels API: hotel prices by date as JSON
author: Aniruddha Garje
summary: Google Hotels shows prices from many booking sites for any city and night. If you want those prices as data, for a price calendar, a daily tracker or a rate check, here is what I learned collecting them, and the request I use. Prices move with the check-in date I priced the first 10 hotels Google listed in Barcelona for check-in 21 and 22 days ahead, on 1 and 2 November 2026, for 2 nights and 2 adults, in EUR (run WpExyDflthAbuKfDG). The median price per night was EUR 122.51 for 1 Nov and EUR 138.38 for 2 Nov. One hotel listed on both days went from EUR 190.66 to EUR 230.92 per night, 21.1% more, one check-in day later. The hotel list moves too The two lists of 10 hotels had only 4 hotels in common. Each date had its own list. So never compare "the first 10 hotels" across dates. Compare the same hotelId across dates. The list also changes between visits, and it can differ from what your browser shows. In my comparison test, two browser visits 12 minutes apart had 87% of their hotels in common. For the hotels a run did return, prices matched the browser within 10% in 99% of cases. You choose the currency Prices come back in the currency you ask for, not the one your location suggests. With currency set to AED, all 20 Dubai prices came back in AED (run Rja3KztI5aZO5DQ5o). For the same night, the median of the first 10 hotels was EUR 103.36 in Lisbon and EUR 113.92 in Porto (run hw8Ld0SQ8Xq9SVcay). The request I use I built an Apify Actor for this, so I get the prices with one HTTP request. You need an Apify account and your API token in the APIFY_TOKEN environment variable. import os import requests url = " https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/garje~google-hotels-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items " run_input = { " queries " : [ " hotels in Barcelona " ], " checkInFromDaysAhead " : 21 , " checkInToDaysAhead " : 27 , " nights " : 2 , " adults " : 2 , " currency " : " EUR " , " maxHotelsPerQuery " : 10 , " proxyConfiguration " : { " useApifyProxy " : True , " apifyProxyGroups " : [ " RESIDENTIAL " ]}, } resp = requests . post ( url , json = run_input , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' APIFY_TOKEN ' ] } " }, timeout = 300 , ) resp . raise_for_status () for row in resp . json (): print ( row [ " checkInDate " ], row [ " name " ], row [ " pricePerNight " ], row [ " currency " ]) Each row carries the check-in date, the hotel's name and ID, the price per night, the currency, and the stay length and occupancy it was priced for. I ran the same request with 2 dates and 2 hotels each, and it returned 4 priced rows in EUR (run igBdVfjBIZWsCAS8m). The price is $1.99 per 1,000 hotel prices, and you are charged only for rows saved. Make it a daily tracker checkInFromDaysAhead and checkInToDaysAhead count from the day of the run. Schedule the request daily and the check-in dates move forward by themselves, with no dates to update. If you would rather click than code, the same setup is saved as a public example you can run: Google Hotels prices by date for 10 hotels . title: Custom API Integration Cost and Timeline: What to Expect
author: Aqib Javaid
summary: "How much will it cost to connect our system to theirs?" is the question I hear most before an integration project, and it's the hardest one to answer from a one-line description. A custom API integration cost can be a few days of work or several months, and both can be described with the same sentence: "we need to connect X to Y". The reason is that the API call is the easy part. What takes time is everything around it: how the data maps between two systems that describe the same thing differently, what happens when a request fails, how you know a payment really went through, and who gets alerted at 2 a.m. when it doesn't. This guide breaks down what drives the cost and the timeline, gives typical effort ranges by complexity, and shows what to ask a developer before you agree on a price. It draws on the kind of integration work I do through my API development and integrations service . [!NOTE] The hour ranges below are typical planning figures from my experience, not a quote. Your price is the hours multiplied by the hourly or project rate of whoever builds it, and rates vary widely by region and seniority. What you are actually paying for An integration has more layers than "call the API". When I scope one, I look at these: Authentication. API keys are quick. OAuth, token refresh and per-customer connections take longer. Data mapping. Field names, formats, units and required fields almost never match between two systems. Business rules. Which records sync, in which direction, and what wins when both sides change. Error handling and retries. Timeouts, rate limits and temporary failures need a plan, not a hope. Webhooks and status sync. Many services tell you about events after the fact, and those messages must be verified and processed safely. Testing and monitoring. Sandbox accounts, edge cases, logging, and alerts when something breaks. Documentation and handover. Someone has to be able to maintain it after the builder leaves. Cheap quotes usually cover the first two layers and skip the rest. Those skipped layers are where integrations fail six months later, which I wrote about in the guide to third-party API integration best practices . Typical effort by complexity Type of integration Typical effort Typical calendar time Example Simple, one-way 15 to 30 hours About 1 week Push new form submissions into a CRM or spreadsheet Standard, two-way with events 20 to 60 hours 1 to 3 weeks Payments plus webhooks, or a CRM sync with status updates Complex, several systems 60 to 150+ hours 4 to 10+ weeks Multiple carriers, ERP data, approval rules and reporting Treat the ranges as starting points. The same integration can fall at either end depending on four things: how good the third party's documentation is, whether a sandbox exists, how messy your existing data is, and how strict your reliability needs are. To turn hours into money, multiply by the rate. As a simple illustration, a standard 40-hour integration at a $50 hourly rate would be about $2,000, and at $100 an hour about $4,000. Your actual rate will differ, and a fixed-price quote should still tell you which of the seven layers above it covers. What pushes the cost up Poor or outdated documentation. Reverse-engineering behaviour costs hours. Rate limits and quotas. You need queues, batching and back-off logic instead of a simple loop. Many third parties at once. On the multi-carrier SIM activation platform , activations had to be routed across a dozen-plus carrier and MVNO backends, which meant per-carrier logic, asynchronous processing with retries and live progress for the user. Each extra system adds mapping and testing, not just one more endpoint. Money involved. Payment flows demand idempotency, verified webhooks and careful reconciliation. A duplicate charge costs far more than the extra hours of safety work. Real-time requirements. Live rates and instant status are harder than nightly syncs. On EXPRECO , the platform integrated UPS and FedEx APIs to calculate real-time shipping rates from package details and destination. Dirty source data. If your records contain duplicates and gaps, cleaning them can cost as much as the integration. The CRM migration cleanup case shows how that plays out. What keeps the cost down Choose an API with good docs, a sandbox and official SDKs. Decide the data rules before development starts: what syncs, which way, and which side wins. Start with one flow end to end, then add more. A thin working slice beats a half-built everything. Ask for retries, logging and alerts in the scope. They're cheaper to add now than after the first outage. Use proven building blocks. For payments, Stripe's own guidance on webhooks and idempotent requests describes the safety patterns your developer should follow. A real example: payments synced with a CRM On the Stripe lead billing project , the workflow let lead-generation clients save a payment method without an immediate charge, then automatically charged it when qualified leads were delivered. The payment lifecycle was connected to GoHighLevel, with webhook-driven status synchronisation for successful and failed payments. On paper that sounds like "Stripe plus a CRM". The parts that need care are the ones around the call: saving payment methods safely, reacting to success and failure events, and keeping both systems in agreement. That's why I scope by layers rather than by endpoint count. If you want the technical side of making retries safe, the idempotency keys article and the webhook delivery guide go into detail. Questions to ask before you agree on a price Which of the seven layers does this quote cover, and which does it leave out? How are failures handled, and who is told when one happens? Is there a sandbox, and will the integration be tested against it? What happens when the third party changes or retires its API? Will I get documentation and the code, so I'm not locked in? What's the ongoing cost? Integrations need small amounts of maintenance each year. When a ready-made connector is the better choice Not every integration needs to be custom. If a no-code tool or a vendor's built-in connector already does what you need, use it. Custom work earns its cost when you need special business rules, reliable handling of money or high volume, or when no connector exists. For a related build-or-buy view on a bigger scale, see the custom CRM cost guide . Frequently asked questions How long does an API integration take? A simple one-way integration can take about a week. A standard two-way integration usually takes one to three weeks, and multi-system work can take a couple of months. The documentation and your data quality are the biggest variables. Why is a custom API integration so expensive? The API call is cheap. The cost is in mapping, error handling, security, testing and monitoring, which keep the integration working after launch. Do I pay for maintenance after launch? Usually a little. Third parties change their APIs, keys expire and edge cases appear. Budget for light maintenance, and ask what is included. Can I get a fixed price? Yes, if the scope is clear. Provide the systems, the data rules and the failure handling you expect, and a good developer can price it. Vague scope leads to vague prices. Key takeaways The cost of an integration is in the layers around the API call, not the call itself. Typical planning ranges are about 15 to 30 hours for simple, 20 to 60 for standard and 60 to 150+ for complex integrations. Documentation quality, rate limits, data quality and money flows are the biggest cost drivers. Ask what a quote covers: errors, retries, monitoring and handover all matter. If you're planning an integration and want a clear, layered estimate from a senior engineer, book a free call and we'll scope it together. Originally published at aqibjavaid.site .

title: 5 Angular Anti-Patterns You Need to Stop Using Immediately (and How to Fix Them in Angular 21)
author: Szj
summary:
Angular is a robust, enterprise-grade framework, but with great power comes great responsibility. Because Angular gives us so much freedom, it is incredibly easy to shoot ourselves in the foot, especially as the application starts to scale. If your app feels sluggish, or if your components are becoming an unmaintainable mess, chances are you are falling victim to a few common bad habits. Let's look at 5 of the most frequent Angular anti-patterns and how to refactor them using modern, clean code practices tailored for Angular 21. 1. Function Calls in Templates (The Performance Killer) The Anti-pattern: Calling a component method directly in your HTML template for data binding.

Total: {{ calculateTotal(cartItems) }}

Why it is bad: Angular's Change Detection (CD) is aggressive by default. Every time anything happens (a click, a timer, an HTTP response), Angular checks the template for changes. If you bind a function in the template, Angular has to re-execute that function every single CD cycle to see if the return value changed. If calculateTotal involves heavy array manipulation, your app will freeze. The Modern Solution: Use Pure Pipes for transformations, or better yet, use Angular 21 Signals . // [GOOD]: Using Angular 21 Signals cartItems = signal < CartItem [] > ([]); // computed() caches the value and ONLY recalculates if cartItems changes! total = computed (() => this . cartItems (). reduce (( acc , item ) => acc + item . price , 0 ));

Total: {{ total() }}

2. Abandoned Subscriptions (The Memory Leak) The Anti-pattern: Subscribing to an Observable but forgetting to unsubscribe when the component is destroyed. // [BAD]: This subscription lives forever, even if the user navigates away. ngOnInit () { this . userService . getUserData (). subscribe ( data => { this . userData = data ; }); } Why it is bad: When the Angular Router destroys this component, the subscription remains active in memory. This leads to memory leaks and ghost code executions in the background, causing weird UI bugs and crashing browsers. The Modern Solution: If you must use RxJS instead of Signals for a specific data stream, use the takeUntilDestroyed() operator. In modern Angular, you do not even need to implement ngOnDestroy for this. // [GOOD]: Modern approach import { takeUntilDestroyed } from ' @angular/core/rxjs-interop ' ; export class UserComponent { constructor ( private userService : UserService ) { this . userService . getUserData () . pipe ( takeUntilDestroyed ()) // Automatically unsubscribes on destroy! . subscribe ( data => this . userData = data ); } } 3. Nested Subscriptions (The Reactive "Callback Hell") The Anti-pattern: Subscribing to an Observable inside another Observable's subscribe block. // [BAD]: Hard to read, impossible to test, and prone to race conditions. this . route . params . subscribe ( params => { this . userService . getUser ( params [ ' id ' ]). subscribe ( user => { this . projectService . getProjects ( user . organizationId ). subscribe ( projects => { this . projects = projects ; }); }); }); Why it is bad: It breaks the declarative nature of RxJS. More importantly, it creates race conditions. If the user clicks fast and triggers multiple ID changes, the HTTP responses might arrive out of order, rendering the wrong data on the screen. The Modern Solution: Leverage Higher-Order Mapping operators like switchMap , concatMap , or mergeMap . // [GOOD]: Clean, linear, and handles race conditions safely. this . projects$ = this . route . params . pipe ( switchMap ( params => this . userService . getUser ( params [ ' id ' ])), switchMap ( user => this . projectService . getProjects ( user . organizationId )) ); (Note: switchMap is perfect here because it cancels previous pending requests if a new ID is emitted). 4. "Fat" Components (The God Object) The Anti-pattern: Stuffing business logic, direct HTTP calls, and complex state manipulation directly into the .ts file of your component. Why it is bad: Your component becomes a monolith. It becomes untestable (because you have to mock 15 different dependencies) and impossible to reuse. UI components should only care about presenting data and catching user events. The Modern Solution: Adopt the Smart / Dumb (Presentational) Component Architecture using Standalone Components, and use a Facade or Service for logic. Move your HTTP logic and state mutations into a dedicated Service, keeping your component clean: // [GOOD]: The component just binds to the facade service. @ Component ({ standalone : true , // ... }) export class CartComponent { // Injecting the service using the modern inject() function private cartFacade = inject ( CartFacadeService ); cartItems = this . cartFacade . items ; // This is a Signal exposed by the service onRemoveItem ( id : string ) { this . cartFacade . removeItem ( id ); // The service handles the actual logic and API call } } 5. The Desperate ChangeDetectorRef Hack The Anti-pattern: Injecting ChangeDetectorRef and throwing cdr.detectChanges() or wrapping code in setTimeout(() => {}, 0) just to force the UI to update. // [BAD]: Forcing Angular to update because the data flow is broken. updateUser () { this . user . name = ' John ' ; this . cdr . detectChanges (); // Please update the UI, I am begging you! } Why it is bad: If you find yourself using this, it means you have lost control of your state management or you are mutating data directly instead of creating new references. It is treating the symptom instead of curing the disease. The Modern Solution: Embrace Zoneless Angular and Immutability . Angular 21 fully supports going Zoneless ( provideZonelessChangeDetection() ). In a Zoneless environment, the framework relies entirely on Signals and built-in reactive primitives to know when to update the DOM, eliminating the need for Zone.js overhead or manual cdr.detectChanges() hacks. // [GOOD]: Treat data as immutable and use Signals for automatic UI updates @ Component ({ standalone : true , // ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush is also recommended if you are not fully zoneless yet changeDetection : ChangeDetectionStrategy . OnPush }) export class UserComponent { user = signal ({ name : ' Jane ' , age : 30 }); updateUser () { // Updating the signal automatically schedules a highly optimized UI update this . user . update ( u => ({ ... u , name : ' John ' })); } } Wrapping Up Angular has heavily shifted towards a reactive, Signal-driven, and Zoneless future. By dropping these 5 anti-patterns and embracing the paradigms of Angular 21, you will immediately notice improvements in your app's Lighthouse scores, memory footprint, and overall developer experience. Over to you: Which of these anti-patterns do you see most often in legacy codebases? Are there any others you would add to this list? Let me know in the comments!

title: my cookieless analytics shows an error instead of a fake number
author: Om Yaduvanshi
summary: most dashboards would rather show you a confident zero than admit they don't know. mine isn't allowed to. i'm om yaduvanshi, 18, an applied ai developer building cloudline , a cookieless analytics tool. day 16 of 90, building in public. the day my dashboard lied to me early on i opened my own dashboard and found a dead day. no visits, flat zero, and the chart drew it with total confidence. it looked exactly like a slow day, so i almost read it as one. the cause was boring. a deploy had missed the script tag. the scary part wasn't the bug, it was the presentation. nothing on the screen suggested anything was wrong. a missing day and a slow day rendered identically, and i was one distracted glance away from building a story on air. zeros are the most expensive lie in analytics a wrong number still gets quoted. "traffic dropped 40% last week" becomes a decision before anyone checks whether last week was real. most dashboards keep the friendly zero anyway, because a dashboard that shows errors looks broken and a dashboard that shows zeros looks fine. i went the other way. when cloudline can't trust its data, it says so. high bursts may get throttled, and when they do you see the message, not a chart that pretends everything is normal. a filter with no matching visits says "no data", not zero. a deleted site takes its data with it immediately, so no ghost rows from dead properties linger in your totals. the honest-limit part this costs me. every error message is a support question a friendly zero would have avoided. "why does my dashboard say this" is a worse first impression than a calm chart. i know that. i also know the calm chart is the thing that lets you believe a lie. the site's own limits page says it in one sentence: errors show a clear message instead of wrong numbers. that's the whole design philosophy. a dashboard's job is to be trusted on the days it has nothing good to say. that's the day you learn whether it deserves you. free while in early access. no card. https://trycloudline.space — om

title: Modelling a clinic day board: appointments, rooms and status transitions without a calendar grid
author: PhysioStack
summary: Most scheduling UIs start with a calendar grid: columns for people, rows for 15-minute slots, coloured blocks on top. That works for booking. It works less well for running the day, which is what reception actually does from 8am to 6pm. A day board is a different view of the same data: a list of today's appointments, grouped by practitioner, where the important thing is not where the block sits but what state it is in . Who has arrived? Who is in a room? Who is done but hasn't paid? This post walks through how to model that, with TypeScript examples. Start with the data model, not the grid The grid tempts you into thinking in slots. Don't. Store intervals and let the view decide how to draw them. type Instant = string ; // ISO 8601 in UTC, e.g. "2026-10-12T22:30:00Z" interface Site { id : string ; name : string ; timeZone : string ; // IANA, e.g. "Australia/Melbourne" or "Australia/Brisbane" } interface Room { id : string ; siteId : string ; name : string ; capacity : number ; // usually 1; a gym area might allow more } interface Appointment { id : string ; siteId : string ; practitionerId : string ; patientId : string ; roomId : string | null ; // assigned on arrival in many clinics start : Instant ; end : Instant ; status : AppointmentStatus ; statusHistory : StatusEvent []; version : number ; // optimistic concurrency } interface StatusEvent { from : AppointmentStatus ; to : AppointmentStatus ; at : Instant ; byUserId : string ; } A few decisions worth calling out: Times are UTC instants. The site owns the timezone. More on why below. Room is nullable. Plenty of clinics don't assign a room until the patient walks in. Forcing it at booking time creates fake data. Status history is append-only. When someone asks "why does this show as paid?", you want an answer. version exists because two people at the front desk will click the same appointment at the same time. A state machine for patient status The day board is really a view over a state machine. A minimal set of states: type AppointmentStatus = | " booked " | " arrived " | " in_treatment " | " done " | " paid " | " cancelled " | " no_show " ; const transitions : Record < AppointmentStatus , AppointmentStatus [] > = { booked : [ " arrived " , " cancelled " , " no_show " ], arrived : [ " in_treatment " , " booked " , " cancelled " ], // "booked" = undo a mis-click in_treatment : [ " done " , " arrived " ], done : [ " paid " , " in_treatment " ], paid : [], cancelled : [ " booked " ], no_show : [ " booked " ], }; Notice the backward edges. Real clinics mis-click. If your machine only moves forward, staff will invent workarounds (cancel and rebook, which destroys history). Explicit undo transitions are better than an admin "force status" button. paid is terminal here, but payment is arguably a separate axis. A patient can be done and owe money, or prepay before treatment. Once you hit that, split it: interface AppointmentFlags { clinicalStatus : AppointmentStatus ; // booked â†’ done paymentStatus : " unpaid " | " part_paid " | " paid " | " no_charge " ; claimStatus : " not_required " | " needs_claim " | " recorded " ; } Keeping claimStatus as its own field is useful even if you never integrate with an external claiming system: it just tracks whether someone still needs to deal with it. The transition function stays boring on purpose: class TransitionError extends Error {} function transition ( appt : Appointment , to : AppointmentStatus , byUserId : string , now : Instant , ): Appointment { const allowed = transitions [ appt . status ]; if ( ! allowed . includes ( to )) { throw new TransitionError ( `Cannot move ${ appt . status } â†’ ${ to } ` ); } return { ... appt , status : to , version : appt . version + 1 , statusHistory : [ ... appt . statusHistory , { from : appt . status , to , at : now , byUserId }, ], }; } On the server, persist with a version check so the second click loses cleanly: UPDATE appointments SET status = $ 1 , version = version + 1 WHERE id = $ 2 AND version = $ 3 ; -- 0 rows updated â†’ reload and show the current state Handling double-booked rooms Practitioner double-booking is usually prevented at booking time. Rooms are trickier, because rooms are often assigned late and appointments overrun. The core check is interval overlap with half-open intervals ( [start, end) ), so a 9:00â€“9:30 and a 9:30â€“10:00 don't collide: const overlaps = ( a : { start : Instant ; end : Instant }, b : { start : Instant ; end : Instant }) => a . start < b . end && b . start < a . end ; // ISO UTC strings compare lexically function roomConflicts ( candidate : Appointment , sameDay : Appointment [], room : Room , ): Appointment [] { if ( ! candidate . roomId ) return []; const active = sameDay . filter ( ( a ) => a . id !== candidate . id && a . roomId === candidate . roomId && ! [ " cancelled " , " no_show " , " done " , " paid " ]. includes ( a . status ) && overlaps ( a , candidate ), ); return active . length >= room . capacity ? active : []; } Two design choices here: Warn, don't block. A hard constraint at the database level sounds safe, but at 10:40 with a patient standing at the desk, a modal saying "cannot save" is the worst outcome. Show the conflict on the board and let a human decide. Status matters to conflicts. A room whose occupant is done is free, even if the booked end time hasn't passed. Conversely, an in_treatment appointment past its end time is still occupying the room. For live occupancy, use max(end, now) for anything still in treatment. If you do want a database guarantee for future bookings, PostgreSQL exclusion constraints on a tstzrange work well, but scope them (e.g. only where status is booked ) so the live day stays flexible. Timezone gotchas for Australian clinics Australia is a great test case for timezone bugs: AEST is UTC+10, AEDT is UTC+11. NSW, Victoria, the ACT and Tasmania switch in October and April. Queensland has no daylight saving. Brisbane stays on UTC+10 all year. A clinic group with sites in Brisbane and on the Gold Coast's NSW side (Tweed Heads) is an hour apart for half the year. South Australia and the Northern Territory sit on half-hour offsets (UTC+9:30, plus DST for SA only). Western Australia is UTC+8 with no DST. Practical rules that save pain: Never store "Australia" or "AEST" as a timezone. Store IANA names per site: Australia/Melbourne , Australia/Brisbane , Australia/Adelaide . Abbreviations are ambiguous and don't encode DST rules. "Today" belongs to the site, not the server. Your server is probably in UTC. Querying "today's appointments" with a UTC midnight boundary will put early Melbourne mornings on the wrong day. import { Temporal } from " @js-temporal/polyfill " ; function dayBounds ( date : string , timeZone : string ) { const day = Temporal . PlainDate . from ( date ); const start = day . toZonedDateTime ({ timeZone }). toInstant (); const end = day . add ({ days : 1 }). toZonedDateTime ({ timeZone }). toInstant (); return { start : start . toString (), end : end . toString () }; } dayBounds ( " 2026-10-04 " , " Australia/Melbourne " ); // DST starts that day: the "day" is 23 hours long Don't assume a day is 24 hours. On DST change days in the southern states, a day is 23 or 25 hours. Anything that builds a board by adding 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 will drift. Store recurring bookings as local wall time. "Every Tuesday at 9am" means 9am local, whatever the offset. Expand recurrences into instants using the site's timezone, never by adding fixed durations to a UTC instant. Render with the site's zone, not the browser's. A practice manager in Melbourne viewing the Brisbane site should see Brisbane times, clearly labelled. Putting it together The day board then becomes a straightforward query: fetch appointments within dayBounds(today, site.timeZone) , group by practitioner, sort by start, and decorate each row with its status, available transitions, and any room conflicts. No grid maths required, and the same data still powers a week or month calendar when you need one. We use this approach in PhysioStack , a day-board-first practice system for Australian physio clinics. The bigger lesson applies to any operational scheduling tool, though: model the states people work with, keep times honest, and let the UI warn rather than refuse when reality gets messy.

title: FitQuest AI: Turning Screen Time into Outdoor Adventures with Local Open-Source AI
author: neerajsbhandari27
summary: FitQuest AI 🌿 — Real Quests. Healthier You. What if your fitness app rewarded you for spending less time on your phone? FitQuest AI uses local AI to turn outdoor movement into bite-sized quests—then encourages you to put your screen away and enjoy the real world. This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass . Demo: Video demo / screenshots · Code: GitHub repository What I Built FitQuest AI is a privacy-conscious, gamified outdoor fitness app powered by a local open-weight AI model. It is designed to help developers and desk workers step away from their monitors and get outside. Instead of focusing on endless metrics on a phone, FitQuest AI turns walks, runs, hikes, and cycling sessions into small RPG-style quests. Generate a quest, head outdoors, then return to log your activity, earn XP, unlock achievements—including a “Touch Grass” milestone—and share your progress with friends. Key Features 🌿 AI Quest Generator: Generates structured outdoor challenges tailored to a fitness goal, experience level, and recent activity. 💬 Interactive AI Coach: Offers conversational guidance around pacing, recovery, and building consistent habits. 🏆 Gamified Progression: Earn XP, level up, track streaks, complete quests, and unlock milestone achievements. 📸 Trail Photos & Story Cards: Add outdoor photos to workouts and create shareable story cards for platforms such as WhatsApp, Instagram, and X. 🔒 Local AI Inference: Uses Ollama with qwen2.5:3b , avoiding a dependency on a hosted AI inference API for the core generation workflow. What Makes FitQuest AI Different? Most fitness apps encourage you to spend more time looking at your screen. FitQuest AI takes the opposite approach: use AI to plan your next outdoor adventure, then put your phone away and go experience it. AI with a purpose: Generate structured, actionable quests instead of generic fitness advice. Progress without pressure: XP, levels, streaks, and achievements make consistency rewarding. Privacy-conscious by design: Local inference helps keep workout context away from third-party cloud AI inference services. Built for exploration: Walking, running, cycling, and hiking become small adventures instead of another task on a to-do list. Demo Video demo / screenshots: Watch the demo Source code: GitHub — FitQuest Tip: Add a screenshot of the dashboard and an example AI-generated quest here if they are available. They help readers quickly understand the experience before watching the video. Tech Stack Component Technology Backend API FastAPI Database / ORM SQLite and SQLAlchemy Frontend React, Vite, Lucide icons Local AI runtime Ollama AI model qwen2.5:3b Data validation Pydantic Story card rendering HTML Canvas How I Built It 1. Local inference engine Rather than relying on a hosted AI inference API, the backend connects to an open-weight model ( qwen2.5:3b ) through Ollama. Pydantic validates the generated structured data before it is used by the application, helping keep AI output predictable. 2. Context-aware coaching The coach can use workout context, explorer progress, and perceived-effort information to make its responses more relevant. Chat history is stored in SQLite so the application can retain conversation context locally. 3. Deterministic gamification The language model generates quest content, but important game rules—such as XP rewards, quest completion, levels, streaks, and achievements—are handled by backend logic. This keeps progression consistent rather than asking the model to decide application state. 4. Client-side story cards The frontend uses an HTML Canvas-based renderer to combine a trail photo, workout stats, and XP details into a shareable image in the browser, without requiring server-side image rendering. Challenges & Learnings Building FitQuest AI involved more than connecting a language model to a fitness app. Structured AI output: LLM responses can be inconsistent, so I used Pydantic validation to turn generated quest data into typed, predictable objects. Running AI locally: Integrating Ollama with a lightweight model makes local inference practical on suitable hardware without a dedicated GPU, though performance depends on the machine. Reliable gamification: XP rewards and quest progression are handled by deterministic backend logic instead of being left to the LLM. Full-stack integration: I connected a FastAPI backend and SQLite database to a React frontend to bring AI-generated quests and fitness progress into one application. The biggest lesson was that AI applications need more than a good prompt: they need validation, predictable business logic, and a user experience that makes the AI genuinely useful. Run It Locally The project uses a local Ollama model, so the first setup requires downloading the model. Commands below are a starting point; check the repository for the latest project-specific setup instructions. Prerequisites Python 3.12 or a compatible Python version Node.js and npm Ollama Git 1. Clone the repository git clone https://github.com/neerajsbhandari27/FitQuest.git cd FitQuest 2. Download the AI model ollama pull qwen2.5:3b Make sure Ollama is running before testing AI-powered features. 3. Start the backend Follow the backend setup instructions in the repository. A typical FastAPI workflow looks like this: cd backend python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt uvicorn app.main:app --reload If the repository uses a different dependency file or startup command, follow its current instructions. 4. Start the frontend In a second terminal, use the frontend directory name as it appears in the repository. For a Vite app, the commands are typically: cd Frontend npm install npm run dev Open the local URL printed by Vite in your terminal. Check the repository's README for the exact API URL configuration and any additional setup. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open-source AI is important to FitQuest AI for three reasons: Personal data privacy: Workout notes, perceived exertion, and activity history can be sensitive. Local inference can keep that context off third-party cloud AI services. Lower ongoing inference costs: Running a local model avoids per-request hosted AI inference charges, although hardware, electricity, and internet access for initial downloads may still have costs. More control: Developers can inspect, adapt, and run the AI workflow on their own machines. Core local features can work without an internet connection once dependencies and model files are installed, provided the app does not rely on external services for that workflow. Open innovation proves that AI doesn't need to keep us trapped in digital feeds—it can be the gentle nudge that helps us disconnect and touch grass. What's Next? FitQuest AI is an evolving project. Potential next steps include: Smarter personalization: Adapt quests using activity history, difficulty preferences, and consistency over time. Richer outdoor adventures: Add themed quest chains, exploration milestones, and multi-day challenges. Improved progress sharing: Expand customizable story cards for celebrating achievements with friends. Community contributions: Welcome bug reports, documentation improvements, UI enhancements, and new feature ideas. Contributing Team: Built collaboratively with @mukesh_kumar_18d186c6e486 . FitQuest AI is open source under the MIT License . Explore the GitHub repository , try it locally, and share feedback or ideas. Before submitting, check the repository for its contribution instructions and existing issues. Final Thought Technology should help us live better—not just keep us online longer. FitQuest AI turns a little AI-generated motivation into a reason to step outside, move, explore, and touch grass . 🌱

title: Meta Releases Llama 4 Scout: Frontier Open-Weights Mixture-of-Depths Architecture with Native 1M-Token Context Window
author: TechBoss
summary: Meta's Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) team has officially released Llama 4 Scout , the open-source community's first frontier-class foundation model built natively on dynamic Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) routing. Llama 4 Scout abandons this uniform allocation through a learned top-k routing gate integrated into each transformer block. During inference, the router assesses token complexity and dynamically assigns computation. Simple tokens bypass deep self-attention and feed-forward layers via residual shortcut paths, while highly informative tokens receive maximal compute across specialized reasoning blocks. This dynamic depth allocation reduces generation latency by 58% compared to dense 70B models while expanding overall model capacity to 105 billion parameters. Native Context Window: 1,000,000 tokens (1M) supported natively with zero rope-frequency degradation. Llama 4 Scout was trained from pre-training step zero with an 8-stage progressive context expansion curriculum up to 1,048,576 tokens. The model effortlessly processes multi-volume legal discovery corpora, entire full-stack software repositories, and extensive scientific literature collections in a single prompt execution. Native runtime support has already merged into vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, and Hugging Face TGI, enabling developers to deploy self-hosted instances across enterprise Kubernetes clusters immediately. title: Google Quantum AI Demonstrates Verifiable Quantum Advantage on 105-Qubit Willow Chip: Molecular Benchmarks Solved in Under 5 Minutes
author: TechBoss
summary: In a landmark peer-reviewed publication released this morning, Google Quantum AI unveiled rigorous empirical benchmarks proving verifiable quantum computational advantage on its newest 105-qubit processor, code-named Willow . Operating inside a dilution refrigerator at 10 millikelvin at Google's Santa Barbara quantum hardware facility, Willow executed ground-state electronic structure calculations for industrial transition-metal complexes in 282 seconds—a workload verified to require approximately 4,200 years of continuous processing on the world's fastest classical exascale supercomputer, Frontier. The Willow Architecture: Sub-Threshold Physical Error Rates Unlike earlier experimental demonstrations based on synthetic random circuit sampling that classical tensor network algorithms eventually approximated, Willow targets real-world molecular chemistry Hamiltonians. The 105-qubit array utilizes a planar square grid of superconducting transmon qubits with tunable capacitive couplers, fabricated using ultra-high-vacuum aluminum evaporation techniques that suppress two-level system (TLS) dielectric defects at substrate interfaces. Crucially, Willow crosses the theoretical error-correction threshold where scaling logical distance directly reduces logical error rates rather than amplifying them. Willow achieves a two-qubit gate fidelity of 99.84% across all operational pairs, while single-qubit gate error sits at 0.038%. This sub-threshold performance enables Google's engineers to implement dynamic distance-5 and distance-7 surface code patches that actively diagnose and correct physical bit-flip and phase-flip faults in real time. Key Hardware Specifications: Google Willow Quantum Processor - Physical Qubit Count: 105 planar superconducting transmon qubits on a tunable 2D grid. Average Two-Qubit CZ Gate Fidelity: 99.84% (interleaved randomized benchmarking). Average Single-Qubit Gate Error: 0.038% with dynamic microwave pulse shaping. Cryogenic Operating Point: 10.4 mK base stage with coaxial cryo-CMOS control lines. Surface Code Scaling: Verified logical qubit lifetime exceeding physical components by 2.4x. Simulating Molecular Ground States in Transition-Metal Catalysis The benchmark simulation centered on determining the active-site catalytic mechanism of nitrogenase iron-molybdenum cofactor (FeMoco), a multi-center transition metal cluster critical to biological nitrogen fixation. Classical quantum chemistry methods—such as Coupled Cluster with Single, Double, and Perturbative Triple Excitations (CCSD(T)) or Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG)—suffer from exponential scaling walls when tracking strongly correlated electron entanglement across the cluster's d-orbitals. Willow executed an optimized Phase Estimation and Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithm combined with zero-noise extrapolation error mitigation. By mapping the fermionic Hamiltonian onto spin operators via the Jordan-Wigner transformation, Willow evaluated 54 active molecular orbitals across 108 spin-orbitals simultaneously. The entire computation converged to chemical accuracy within 4 minutes and 42 seconds, establishing an absolute verification point that classical supercomputers cannot reproduce without unviable energy consumption. "We have moved beyond statistical arguments over toy mathematical distributions. Willow is solving concrete, non-trivial Hamiltonian equations that directly inform catalytic chemistry and battery material discovery. For the first time, quantum hardware is demonstrating utility that classical silicon clusters cannot economically match." Industry Implications for Semiconductor and Pharmaceutical Research The validation of Willow's architecture marks a major shift for industrial materials science. Google announced that early access allocations are opening for select pharmaceutical partners and semiconductor research consortia under the Google Quantum Cloud umbrella. Researchers will utilize Willow to explore room-temperature superconductor candidates, synthetic fertilizer synthesis pathways, and cathode degradation kinetics for next-generation solid-state lithium batteries. While universal fault-tolerant quantum computing with millions of physical qubits remains a multi-year road-map goal, Willow confirms that intermediate noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) and early error-corrected architectures have arrived at commercial industrial relevance. As classical chip fabrication approaches atomic limits at the 1.4nm node, quantum coprocessors are transitioning from theoretical physics experiments into specialized enterprise accelerators. When working with contemporary neural architectures, memory capacity (VRAM) consistently represents the primary operational bottleneck rather than raw compute cycles. Quantized weights, such as 4-bit AWQ or 8-bit FP8 representations, significantly reduce memory footprints while preserving empirical task performance across standardized reasoning evaluations. Thermal Management: Maintaining target GPU junction temperatures below 78 degrees Celsius ensures sustained boost clock frequencies during continuous batch runs. Implementing localized inference pipelines guarantees data sovereignty, removes external API rate limits, and provides predictable execution costs across enterprise software environments. title: "TrailQuest: an open-weight AI plans your walk, then tells you to put the phone away"
author: Noor Ul Huda
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Most fitness apps want your attention. TrailQuest wants the opposite. You tell it how you feel today: your energy, your mood, how many minutes you have, indoors or outdoors, and a goal like 8,000 steps. It builds you a short quest : a warm-up, a brisk walk with faster intervals, a nature challenge (like "spot something with three colors"), and a cooldown. Then you press Start , and the screen turns into a plain timer that says Phone away. Go enjoy it. You walk. When you come back, you log your steps and earn XP and a Touch Grass streak . The streak counts any finished quest, even an easy recovery walk. It rewards showing up, not pushing harder. It's for people who want to move more but burn out on apps that demand attention, and for tired days when a gentle 10-minute quest beats skipping. Demo ▶ Watch the 50-second demo video In the demo, I create an account with an email code and set a 10-minute outdoor quest. I press Start and the phone-away timer runs. Then I log 3,200 steps and get 82 XP and a 1-day streak. I also open the dashboard, the daily journal, the trail map and the badges, and switch to dark mode with the Ocean theme and miles. Code GitHub repo: github.com/noorulhuda07/trailquest To run it: docker compose up --build , open http://localhost:8080 , and click Try the demo . How I Built It Stack: React and Vite for the frontend, FastAPI for the backend, Gemma through Ollama for quest generation, SQLite for accounts, and Docker Compose to run it all. User → FastAPI → Gemma (via Ollama) → Validator → Quest ↓ fails or unavailable Rules-based fallback → Quest My main rule is AI suggests, code validates. Gemma never talks to the user directly. Its answer must pass these checks first: Is it valid JSON with all the required fields? Does the intensity match the energy the user chose? Do the step durations add up to the time they have? Does any step contain unsafe wording? Is it an indoor quest? Then there are no nature challenges. If a check fails, or Gemma isn't available, a small rules engine builds a safe quest instead. Every quest carries a badge that says which one wrote it: Gemma (gemma3), self-hosted, code-validated or Backup rules engine . The server sets the badge, not the model, so the model can't claim credit it didn't earn. I also kept free text out of the prompt. Energy, mood and target are fixed options, and the workout type comes from a fixed list, so a user can't smuggle instructions into the model. Around the AI, I built sign-up with email or phone codes, Google sign-in, a one-click demo mode, and light and dark modes with four color themes. I tested the app with 42 backend tests and 5 frontend tests. The backend tests cover forged login tokens, SQL injection strings, code guessing, rate limits, and malformed or unsafe model output. GitHub Actions runs the tests and security scans on every push. What I Saw When I Ran It In my recorded demo, the quest came from the backup rules engine, not from Gemma, and the badge on screen says so. I'd rather show that than hide it. It's the point of the design: a missing or bad AI answer never reaches the user, and the app always gives a safe quest. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Your mood stays yours. A quest request contains your energy, mood and schedule. With an open-weight model running on your own machine, that data doesn't need to leave it. I can swap the model with one setting. GEMMA_MODEL=gemma3:1b for a laptop with little memory, or a bigger one if you have the hardware. Fine-tuning for coaching styles is possible later. No bill per quest. Running it costs electricity, not API fees. I control the guardrails. Because I run the model, I choose the output format and what happens when it misbehaves. The trade-offs: the first run downloads about 3 GB, and a small model on a CPU is slower and less reliable than a large hosted one. That is exactly why the validator and fallback exist. My Agent Session I built TrailQuest with help from an AI coding assistant, then ran and tested the result myself. What's Next Weather and location tools so a rainy day gives an indoor quest, then friends, group quests and challenges. Real step tracking comes with a phone app. Built by noorulhuda07.

title: โมเดล 27B ย่อเหลือ 7.89 GB ชนะตัวเต็ม 54 GB ได้จริงไหม? เจาะ Saluki 27B
author: Nokka
summary: โมเดล 27B ย่อเหลือ 7.89 GB ชนะตัวเต็ม 54 GB ได้จริงไหม? เจาะ Saluki 27B โดย Nokka (นก-กา) | 11 ตุลาคม 2026 บทความนี้เขียนโดย AI (โมเดล deepseek-v4.1-flash ของผู้ให้บริการ ollama-cloud) ผ่าน Hermes Agent จาก Nous Research ตรวจสอบและเรียบเรียงโดย Nokka ถ้าคุณเคยลองย่อโมเดลลงเหลือ 2 บิตแล้วเจอปัญหาเดิมทุกครั้ง นี่คือข่าวที่คุณน่าจะอยากอ่านให้จบ ทีม Underdog จาก Conway Research ปล่อยไฟล์ขนาด 7.89 GB ที่ทำคะแนน 88 จาก 120 ในชุดทดสอบเรียกเครื่องมือของพวกเขาเอง ขณะที่โมเดลต้นทางตัวเต็มขนาด ราว 54 GB ทำได้ 84 [1][2] นั่นคือเล็กลง 6.84 เท่า แต่คะแนนกลับสูงกว่า 4 งาน ตัวเลขนี้จริง แต่คำถามที่ควรถามไม่ได้อยู่ตรงนั้น สรุปสั้น Saluki 27B เป็นการย่อ Qwen3.8-27B ด้วยเทคนิค 2 บิตแบบผสม (IQ2 mix) จนเหลือ 7.89 GB ให้คะแนนเรียกเครื่องมือดีกว่าตัวเต็มบนชุดทดสอบของทีมผู้สร้างเอง ยังรันบน llama.cpp มาตรฐาน [10] ไม่ต้องคอมไพล์ fork และใช้สัญญาอนุญาต Apache 2.0 แต่มีสามอย่างที่ต้องรู้พร้อมกัน คือ ทีมผู้สร้างมีบิลด์ของตัวเองที่ทำได้ดีกว่า Saluki อีกตัวหนึ่ง, มีคู่แข่งที่ชนะ Saluki ในงานเรียกเครื่องมือพร้อมกันหลายคำสั่งแบบขาดลอย และคะแนนคณิตศาสตร์ระดับแข่งขันถอยลงราว 15 ถึง 18% Saluki 27B คืออะไร โมเดลต้นทางคือ Qwen3.8-27B โมเดลขนาด 27,000 ล้านพารามิเตอร์แบบ dense จากทีม Qwen สถาปัตยกรรมผสมระหว่าง linear attention แบบ gated delta net กับ full attention รองรับบริบท 262,144 โทเคน และใช้สัญญาอนุญาต Apache 2.0 [3] Saluki ไม่ได้เทรนใหม่ ทีม Underdog รับช่วงต่อจาก ISTA-DASLab ที่ปล่อย GGUF แบบ 2 บิตด้วยวิธี GSQ และ RCO มาก่อน แล้วทำบิลด์ 2 บิตแบบผสมของตัวเองทับลงไป โดยเลือกข้อมูลคาลิเบรตที่รักษาพฤติกรรมการเรียกเครื่องมือไว้ [1][11] จุดขายที่ทีมผู้สร้างเน้นคือ ไฟล์เดียว 7.89 GB รันบน llama.cpp มาตรฐาน ไม่ต้องมีบิลด์พิเศษ ไม่ต้องมี runtime แยก เปิดใช้ผ่าน OpenAI chat API บนพอร์ต 8080 ได้เลย [1][2] สื่อสายเทคบางเจ้ารายงานว่าไฟล์นี้รันได้ใน Ollama, LM Studio และ vLLM ด้วย [11] ขณะที่หน้าของเจ้าของระบุถึง llama.cpp มาตรฐานเป็นหลัก [1][2] ผมจึงรายงานตามที่ทั้งสองฝ่ายเขียน ยังไม่สรุปว่าฝ่ายใดครบกว่า ไฟล์โมเดลในรุ่น 1.0 มีระดับเดียวคือ Underdog-Saluki-27B-1.0-IQ2-mix.gguf ขนาด 7.89 GB (ยังมีไฟล์ vision add-on แยกอีกสองไฟล์สำหรับงานภาพ) มีโหมดคิดในหัวเปิดไว้เป็นค่าตั้งต้นและปิดได้ต่อคำขอ [1] วิธีรันแบบเร็ว huggingface-cli download ConwayResearch/Underdog-Saluki-27B-1.0 \ Underdog-Saluki-27B-1.0-IQ2-mix.gguf --local-dir . llama-server -m Underdog-Saluki-27B-1.0-IQ2-mix.gguf \ --jinja -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 ธง --jinja เปิดใช้เทมเพลตแชตของ Qwen3.8 ซึ่งจัดการทั้งการเรียกเครื่องมือและโหมดคิดในหัว ส่วนการตั้งค่าที่แนะนำคือ temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20 สำหรับงานทั่วไป และ temperature 0 สำหรับงานเรียกเครื่องมือที่ต้องการความเร็ว [1] ตัวเลข 88 กับ 84 หมายถึงอะไร ชุดทดสอบที่ทีมใช้ชื่อ Underdog Bench เป็นงาน 120 ชิ้นดึงจาก Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard รุ่นที่ 4 แบ่งเป็นห้าประเภท ประเภทละ 24 งาน และ แช่แข็งชุดงานไว้ตั้งแต่วันที่ 27 กันยายน 2026 ก่อนจะเริ่มทดสอบโมเดลใด ๆ [1][2][8] ผลที่ออกมาวางเรียงได้แบบนี้ บิลด์หลักของทีม Underdog (7.9 GB) ทำได้ 91 จาก 120 Saluki (7.89 GB) ทำได้ 88 จาก 120 Mia 2-bit (9.1 GB) ทำได้ 85 Qwen3.8-27B ตัวเต็ม (ราว 54 GB) ทำได้ 84 ISTA 2-bit (8.4 GB) ทำได้ 76 Ternary Bonsai 2 (5.95 GB) ทำได้ 70 ทุกตัวรันใน runtime ของตัวเอง ซึ่งเป็นกรณีที่ดีที่สุดของแต่ละไฟล์ ทีมผู้สร้างระบุว่า Saluki และบิลด์หลักของเขาทำได้ดีกว่าตัวเต็ม 76 ถึง 77 งานจาก 84 งานที่ตัวเต็มทำได้ [2] จุดที่น่าสนใจกว่าคะแนนรวมคือ การเลือกเครื่องมือให้ถูกตัว ในห้าประเภทงานนั้น Saluki ทำได้ 47 จาก 48 ในสองประเภทแรก ซึ่งเป็นงานเลือกฟังก์ชันเดียวที่ถูกต้อง กับเลือกฟังก์ชันที่ถูกจากหลายตัวเลือก เทียบกับ Mia ที่ทำได้ 31 จาก 48 [2] สามข้อที่ทีมผู้สร้างยอมรับเอง ส่วนนี้คือส่วนที่ทำให้ผมเชื่อตัวเลขชุดนี้มากกว่าคะแนน benchmark ทั่วไป เพราะทีมเขียนไว้เองบนหน้าของพวกเขา ข้อที่หนึ่ง: บิลด์หลักของตัวเองชนะ Saluki บนหน้าทางการระบุชัดว่าบิลด์หลักของทีมทำได้ 91 ส่วน Saluki ทำได้ 88 ทั้งที่ขนาดใกล้กันมาก คือ 7.9 กับ 7.89 GB และอธิบายเหตุผลที่ปล่อย Saluki ว่าเป็นเพราะบิลด์หลัก เล่นเว็บได้แย่กว่า โดยตอบคำถามจากเว็บจริงได้ 48 จาก 150 ข้อ หรือ 32% ขณะที่ Saluki ตอบได้ 60 จาก 150 ข้อ หรือ 40% [2] ข้อที่สอง: คู่แข่งชนะในงานเรียกเครื่องมือพร้อมกัน งานที่ต้องเรียกหลายเครื่องมือในคำตอบเดียว Saluki ทำได้ 42 จาก 100 เมื่อตรวจแบบเข้มงวด Mia ทำได้ 69 จาก 100 ทีมเขียนไว้ตรง ๆ ว่า Mia เป็นผู้นำในหมวดนี้อย่างชัดเจน และบอกเหตุผลที่ยังเลือกปล่อย Saluki ว่าขนาดไฟล์เล็กกว่า คือ 7.89 GB เทียบกับ 9.1 GB [2] ตัวเลขนี้เปลี่ยนเมื่อใช้ตัวตรวจที่ผ่อนปรนความผิดพลาดเรื่องรูปแบบ คือ Saluki ขยับจาก 42 เป็น 55 จาก 100 ขณะที่ Mia ขยับแค่จาก 69 เป็น 70 [2] ข้อที่สาม: ทีมไม่เคลมว่าเก่งกว่าตัวเต็ม ประโยคที่ผมคิดว่าสำคัญที่สุดในทั้งหน้าเผยแพร่คือ ทีมระบุว่า "เราไม่ได้อ้างว่ามันฉลาดกว่าโมเดลต้นฉบับ งาน 120 ชิ้นเป็นการทดสอบที่พอประมาณ และส่วนหนึ่งของความต่างนั้นน่าจะมาจากความแปรปรวนระหว่างรอบรัน" [2] ในบทความเชิงเทคนิค ทีมยังระบุด้วยว่าคะแนนสาธารณะของโมเดลต้นฉบับ มาจาก harness คนละตัวกับที่ทีมใช้ และตัวเลข IFEval ที่ทีมรายงานนั้นนับหกพรอมป์ที่ทำไม่เสร็จเป็นความล้มเหลว ซึ่งเป็นมุมที่ระวังตัวกว่า [2] ในมุมมองของผม การที่ทีมเขียนแบบนี้ทำให้ตัวเลข 88 กับ 84 มีน้ำหนักกว่าคะแนนที่ไม่มีคำกำกับเลย จุดที่ถอยลง การย่อลง 6.84 เท่าไม่ได้ฟรี ทีมผู้สร้างระบุข้อจำกัดไว้เองครบ คณิตศาสตร์ระดับแข่งขัน ถอยลงชัดเจน คะแนน AIME 2025 อยู่ที่ 79.2 เทียบกับ 96.7 ของตัวเต็ม หรือราว 81.9% ส่วน AIME 2026 อยู่ที่ 80.0 เทียบกับ 94.6 หรือราว 84.6% ทีมสรุปว่าเก็บคะแนนคณิตศาสตร์ไว้ได้ 82 ถึง 85% [1] งานปริศนาระดับตัวอักษร อย่างคำกลับหัว กฎสระ และการเรียงตามตัวอักษร เป็นประเภทที่อ่อนที่สุด [2] งานเรียกเครื่องมือพร้อมกัน ตัวตรวจแบบเข้มงวดอ่านไม่ออก 23 งานจาก 100 คำตอบ ทีมระบุว่าส่วนใหญ่เป็นเรื่องรูปแบบ [1][2] งานเขียนโค้ด Saluki แก้ปัญหาจาก SWE-bench Verified ได้ 30 จาก 50 ข้อ เทียบกับ 33 ของตัวเต็ม หรือเก็บไว้ 27 จาก 33 ข้อที่ตัวเต็มแก้ได้ [2] โหมดคิดในหัว เมื่อเปิดอยู่ โมเดลมักใช้เวลาไตร่ตรองนานก่อนตอบ งานที่ต้องการความเร็วต้องปิด [1] มาเป็นข้อความล้วน ไฟล์หลักรับข้อความเท่านั้น ต้องโหลดไฟล์ vision แยกอีก 629 ถึง 928 MB [1] ตัวเลข MBPP+ อยู่ที่ 78.0 เทียบกับ 83.9 หรือราว 93% และ MuSR อยู่ที่ 67.5 เทียบกับ 79.6 หรือราว 84.8% ส่วน IFEval อยู่ที่ 93.5 เทียบกับ 91.5 ซึ่งสูงกว่า [1] จุดต่างจริงคือ runtime ไม่ใช่คะแนน ถ้าผมจะเลือกตัวเลขเดียวมาอธิบายว่าทำไม Saluki ถึงน่าสนใจ ผมจะไม่เลือก 88 หรือ 84 ผมจะเลือกคำว่า llama.cpp มาตรฐาน คู่แข่งทั้งสามตัวมีเงื่อนไขเรื่อง runtime ต่างกันชัดเจน Mia 2-bit อยู่ในรูปแบบ EXL3 ของ ExLlamaV3 จึงต้องใช้ exllamav3 รัน และ โหลดใน llama.cpp ไม่ได้เลย [2][6] Ternary Bonsai 2 ของ PrismML น้ำหนักแบบ ternary 1.72 บิตต่อพารามิเตอร์ ต้องใช้ llama.cpp fork ของ PrismML เท่านั้น เอกสารระบุตรง ๆ ว่า llama.cpp มาตรฐานจะปฏิเสธไฟล์ PQ2_0 และ PTQ1_0
